## Intuition

In **control theory** we steer a dynamical system by choosing an input (the
**control**) over time so as to optimize a payoff. It is an individual
decision problem: there are no competing players, which distinguishes it from
[[game-theory]]. When the dynamics contain randomness the payoff is an
expectation and we are in [[stochastic-control]].

The central idea is that we optimize over a *function* (the control path), an
infinite dimensional problem, which is why the tools come from the
[[calculus-of-variations]] ([[euler-lagrange-equation]], Hamilton's equations,
[[hamilton-jacobi-equation]]).

## Problem formulation

:::{.definition data-title="Controlled system"}

Let $A\subset\mathbb{R}^m$ be a compact set of **admissible control values**.
A **control** is a (measurable) function $\alpha:[0,T]\to A$. Given
$f:\mathbb{R}^n\times A\to\mathbb{R}^n$ (written
$f(x,a,t)$ if it depends on time), the **controlled dynamical system** is
$$
\begin{cases}
\dot{x}(s)=f(x(s),\alpha(s)), & s\in[t,T],\\
x(t)=x,
\end{cases}
$$
started at time $t$ from state $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$. It is **autonomous** when
$f$ has no explicit time dependence.

:::

The dynamics are Markovian: the change of state from $s$ to $s+h$ depends
only on the current state $x(s)$ and current control $\alpha(s)$, as in the
action of a discrete-time Markov decision process (see
[[markov-chains]]).

:::{.definition data-title="Payoff functional"}

The **payoff** (a [[calculus-of-variations|functional]] of the control) is
$$
P_{t,x}[\alpha]=\int_{t}^{T}r(x(s),\alpha(s))\,ds+g(x(T)),
$$
where $r$ is the **running payoff** and $g$ the **terminal payoff**.

:::

The **optimal control problem** is to find $\alpha^*$ with
$P_{t,x}[\alpha^*]\geq P_{t,x}[\alpha]$ for every admissible $\alpha$. In
practice we require $f$, $r$, $g$ to be regular, e.g.
[[lipschitz-continuity|Lipschitz continuous]], so that the ODE is well posed.

:::{.example data-title="Staying near the origin"}

An individual starts at the origin of a line and is rewarded for being close
to it after one minute, while moving at speed at most 1. Then
$\dot{x}=\alpha$, $x(0)=0$, $A=[-1,1]$, $r=0$, $g(x)=-|x|$, so
$P[\alpha]=-|x(1)|$ is to be maximized. The optimal strategy is $\alpha\equiv0$.

:::

## Value function and dynamic programming

:::{.definition data-title="Value function"}

The **value function** is the best attainable payoff from state $x$ at time
$t$:
$$
u(x,t)=\sup_{\alpha}P_{t,x}[\alpha],\qquad u(x,T)=g(x).
$$

:::

The value function obeys the [[dynamic-programming-principle]]: for
$t\le t+h\le T$,
$$
u(x,t)=\sup_{\alpha}\left\{\int_{t}^{t+h}r(x(s),\alpha(s))\,ds
+u(x(t+h),t+h)\right\}.
$$
Letting $h\to0$ formally yields the first-order PDE
$$
-\partial_{t}u(x,t)=\sup_{a\in A}\left\{f(x,a)\cdot\nabla u(x,t)+r(x,a)\right\},
$$
a [[hamilton-jacobi-equation]] with Hamiltonian
$H(x,p)=\sup_{a}\{f(x,a)\cdot p+r(x,a)\}$ (see [[hamiltonian-mechanics]],
[[gradient]]). In the stochastic case a second-order term appears, giving the
[[hjb-equation]].

## Methods

- **Calculus of variations / Pontryagin**: necessary conditions for an
  optimal path via Hamilton's equations (see [[hamiltonian-mechanics]]) and
  [[lagrange-multiplier-method]] for the dynamic constraint.
- **Dynamic programming**: solve the Hamilton-Jacobi(-Bellman) equation for
  $u$, then choose $\alpha^*(s)$ as a maximizer of the Hamiltonian along the
  optimal trajectory.
